lesson.title: Arcsec and the Case for Absolute Value
lesson.summary: Differentiating arcsec x forces a subtlety that arcsin, arccos, and arctan never raised: the sign of the derivative depends on the sign of x, which is exactly why an absolute value appears in the formula.
lesson.body:
Secant is not one to one on any single familiar interval without leaving a gap, since sec y is undefined at y = pi/2. The standard fix is to restrict secant to the two piece domain [0, pi/2) union (pi/2, pi], where it is one to one and covers every value with |x| >= 1. Its inverse, y = arcsec x, is defined exactly for |x| >= 1.

Differentiating implicitly from sec y = x gives sec y tan y times y' = 1, so y' = 1/(sec y tan y) = 1/(x tan y). To finish, tan y needs to be written in terms of x. From tan^2 y = sec^2 y - 1 = x^2 - 1, tan y = plus or minus sqrt(x^2-1), and the sign depends on which piece of the domain y is in. On [0, pi/2), x = sec y >= 1 and tan y >= 0, so tan y = sqrt(x^2-1), giving y' = 1/(x sqrt(x^2-1)), which is positive, matching x > 0. On (pi/2, pi], x = sec y <= -1, and here sin y >= 0 while cos y < 0, so tan y <= 0, meaning tan y = -sqrt(x^2-1). Substituting gives y' = 1/(x times -sqrt(x^2-1)) = -1/(x sqrt(x^2-1)), and since x is negative on this piece, -1/x equals 1/|x|, so this again equals 1/(|x| sqrt(x^2-1)). Both pieces agree on a single formula: d/dx[arcsec x] = 1/(|x| sqrt(x^2-1)), which is always positive, consistent with arcsec increasing on each piece of its domain.

For practice, differentiate y = arcsec(2x), defined where |2x| >= 1, meaning |x| >= 1/2. With u = 2x and u' = 2, the chain rule gives dy/dx = u'/(|u| sqrt(u^2-1)) = 2/(|2x| sqrt(4x^2-1)) = 2/(2|x| sqrt(4x^2-1)) = 1/(|x| sqrt(4x^2-1)). At x = 1, this gives 1/sqrt(3), a positive number, as expected.

The two piece case analysis above is the whole reason the absolute value exists in this formula. The exact same pattern reappears in the next chapter for arccsc, which is built the same way from the two piece domain of cosecant.
